# 14 Hydrocarbons

本章只覆盖 AS 3.2 Hydrocarbons：alkanes、alkenes、crude oil、cracking、combustion、free-radical substitution、electrophilic addition、oxidation 和 addition polymerisation。题目均来自 **3.2 Hydrocarbons** 原题；不能独立提取的题图未使用截图替代。

## Learning objectives

- explain alkane unreactivity and free-radical substitution;
- describe fractional distillation, cracking and combustion of hydrocarbon fuels;
- apply electrophilic addition reactions of alkenes;
- use bromine water and manganate(VII) reactions to identify C=C;
- explain addition polymerisation and environmental effects of vehicle emissions.

## 14.1 Alkanes and free-radical substitution

Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>. They are relatively unreactive because C–C and C–H bonds have high bond enthalpies and are almost non-polar. They undergo combustion and, with halogens under UV light, free-radical substitution.

For chlorination of methane:

<div class="equation-block">Initiation: Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2Cl·<br>Propagation: Cl· + CH<sub>4</sub> → HCl + CH<sub>3</sub>·<br>Propagation: CH<sub>3</sub>· + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>Cl + Cl·<br>Termination: CH<sub>3</sub>· + CH<sub>3</sub>· → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub></div>

Initiation makes radicals, propagation uses and regenerates a radical, and termination removes radicals. Homolytic fission splits the bonding pair equally: Cl–Cl → 2Cl·.

## 14.2 Crude oil, fractionation and cracking

Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons, mainly alkanes. Fractional distillation separates fractions by boiling point: larger molecules have stronger London forces and higher boiling points. A fraction contains hydrocarbons with a range of chain lengths, not one pure compound.

**Cracking** breaks larger saturated hydrocarbons into smaller, more useful molecules, producing alkanes and alkenes. It is carried out by vaporising the fraction and passing it over a hot catalyst such as alumina/silica, or by strong heating. It meets demand for small fuel molecules and for alkene feedstock. For example:

<div class="equation-block">C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> → C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> + C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub></div>

## 14.3 Alkenes and electrophilic addition

Alkenes contain C=C and have general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub> for an open-chain molecule with one double bond. The π bond is electron-rich and weaker than the σ bond, so it reacts with electrophiles. In electrophilic addition, the alkene first donates π electrons to an electrophile, forming a carbocation; a negative ion then bonds to the positive carbon.

| Reagent and conditions | Product / observation |
|---|---|
| Br<sub>2</sub> in organic solvent | dibromoalkane; bromine decolourises |
| Br<sub>2</sub>(aq) | bromoalcohol and dibromoalkane |
| steam, phosphoric acid catalyst, 600 K, high pressure | alcohol |
| HBr | bromoalkane; unsymmetrical alkenes may give major/minor products |
| H<sub>2</sub>, Ni, heat | alkane |
| cold dilute acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> | vicinal diol; purple decolourises |
| hot concentrated acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> | oxidative cleavage of C=C |

The more stable carbocation is formed more readily; this explains the major product in addition of HBr to an unsymmetrical alkene.

## 14.4 Combustion, emissions and catalytic converters

Complete combustion has excess oxygen and makes CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O. Incomplete combustion, when oxygen is limited, produces CO and/or carbon. Carbon monoxide binds strongly to haemoglobin and reduces oxygen transport. High-temperature engines also form NO<sub>x</sub>; NO<sub>x</sub> and unburnt hydrocarbons contribute to photochemical smog.

Catalytic converters use redox reactions to reduce NO<sub>x</sub> to N<sub>2</sub> and oxidise CO/hydrocarbons to CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O, for example 2CO + 2NO → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + N<sub>2</sub>.

## 14.5 Addition polymerisation

In addition polymerisation, many alkene monomers join when the C=C opens, forming only C–C σ bonds in the backbone. The repeat unit is shown in brackets with continuation bonds, for example poly(propene): [–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–]<sub>n</sub>. No small molecule is eliminated.

## Multiple choice questions

::: {.mc-question #hc-mc-01 data-answer="B"}
### Question 1 · 3.2 Choice Easy Q1
<p>Which equation represents a valid propagation step in the free radical reaction between ethane and chlorine?</p>
<div class="mc-options"><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="A"><strong>A</strong><span>C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + Cl· → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl + H·</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="B"><strong>B</strong><span>C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl + Cl· → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>Cl· + HCl</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="C"><strong>C</strong><span>C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + H· → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>· + HCl</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="D"><strong>D</strong><span>C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>· + Cl· → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl</span></button></div>
<button class="check-answer">Check answer</button><p class="mc-feedback"></p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p><strong>B.</strong> It consumes one radical and forms one radical. D is termination because radicals are destroyed.</p></details>
:::

::: {.mc-question #hc-mc-02 data-answer="B"}
### Question 2 · 3.2 Choice Easy Q2
<p>A fraction of distilled crude oil contains molecules with between 15 and 19 carbon atoms. This fraction is cracked by strong heating. Why is this done?<br>1 To produce alkenes. 2 To produce smaller molecules which are in higher demand. 3 To insert oxygen atoms into the hydrocarbons.</p>
<div class="mc-options"><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="A"><strong>A</strong><span>1, 2 and 3</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="B"><strong>B</strong><span>1 and 2</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="C"><strong>C</strong><span>2 and 3</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="D"><strong>D</strong><span>1 only</span></button></div><button class="check-answer">Check answer</button><p class="mc-feedback"></p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p><strong>B.</strong> Cracking produces smaller hydrocarbons including alkenes; it does not insert oxygen.</p></details>
:::

::: {.mc-question #hc-mc-03 data-answer="B"}
### Question 3 · 3.2 Choice Easy Q3
<p>Ethene reacts with steam in the presence of sulfuric acid: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH. What type of reaction is this?</p>
<div class="mc-options"><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="A"><strong>A</strong><span>acid/base</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="B"><strong>B</strong><span>addition</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="C"><strong>C</strong><span>hydrolysis</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="D"><strong>D</strong><span>substitution</span></button></div><button class="check-answer">Check answer</button><p class="mc-feedback"></p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p><strong>B.</strong> H and OH add across the C=C.</p></details>
:::

::: {.mc-question #hc-mc-04 data-answer="C"}
### Question 4 · 3.2 Choice Easy Q4
<p>Which statements about alkenes are correct?<br>1 They are less reactive than alkanes towards electrophiles. 2 They are used as monomers for polymerisation. 3 They are formed when higher alkanes are cracked.</p>
<div class="mc-options"><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="A"><strong>A</strong><span>1, 2 and 3</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="B"><strong>B</strong><span>1 and 2</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="C"><strong>C</strong><span>2 and 3</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="D"><strong>D</strong><span>3 only</span></button></div><button class="check-answer">Check answer</button><p class="mc-feedback"></p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p><strong>C.</strong> Alkenes are more reactive towards electrophiles because of their π bond.</p></details>
:::

::: {.mc-question #hc-mc-05 data-answer="D"}
### Question 5 · 3.2 Choice Easy Q5
<p>One catalytic-converter reaction is between nitrogen oxide and octane. Which equation gives only non-toxic products?</p>
<div class="mc-options"><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="A"><strong>A</strong><span>C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> + 16NO → 8CO + 8N<sub>2</sub> + 9H<sub>2</sub>O</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="B"><strong>B</strong><span>C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> + 24NO → 8CO<sub>2</sub> + 12N<sub>2</sub> + 8H<sub>2</sub>O</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="C"><strong>C</strong><span>C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> + 17NO → 8CO + 8½N<sub>2</sub> + 9H<sub>2</sub>O</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="D"><strong>D</strong><span>C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> + 25NO → 8CO<sub>2</sub> + 12½N<sub>2</sub> + 9H<sub>2</sub>O</span></button></div><button class="check-answer">Check answer</button><p class="mc-feedback"></p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p><strong>D.</strong> It is balanced and gives CO<sub>2</sub>, N<sub>2</sub> and water, rather than toxic CO.</p></details>
:::

::: {.mc-question #hc-mc-06 data-answer="A"}
### Question 6 · 3.2 Choice Easy Q6
<p>When bromine reacts with propene in an organic solvent at room temperature, what is the mechanism by which bromine attacks the propene?</p>
<div class="mc-options"><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="A"><strong>A</strong><span>electrophilic addition</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="B"><strong>B</strong><span>electrophilic substitution</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="C"><strong>C</strong><span>nucleophilic addition</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="D"><strong>D</strong><span>nucleophilic substitution</span></button></div><button class="check-answer">Check answer</button><p class="mc-feedback"></p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p><strong>A.</strong> The alkene π bond attacks polarised Br<sub>2</sub>.</p></details>
:::

### Question 7 · 3.2 Choice Easy Q7
![Polymer sequence used to identify the monomer](../assets/questions/extracted/14/independent/choice-easy-q7-polymer.png){.question-figure fig-alt="Displayed polymer chain with chlorine substituents"}
<p>Which monomer could produce a polymer with repeating unit –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH(Cl)–?</p>
<div class="mc-options"><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="A"><strong>A</strong><span>CHCl=CHCl</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="B"><strong>B</strong><span>CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCl</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="C"><strong>C</strong><span>CH<sub>3</sub>CCl=CHCl</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="D"><strong>D</strong><span>CH<sub>3</sub>CCl=CH<sub>2</sub></span></button></div><button class="check-answer">Check answer</button><p class="mc-feedback"></p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p><strong>B.</strong> Addition polymerisation opens the double bond while retaining the Cl substituent.</p></details>

### Question 8 · 3.2 Choice Easy Q8
<p>Four students made statements about alkanes and alkenes. W: bromine reacts with alkanes by electrophilic substitution. X: bromine reacts with alkenes by a free-radical addition mechanism. Y: alkenes can be oxidised by acidified manganate(VII) ions. Z: alkenes are formed from alkanes by cracking. Which two students are correct?</p>
<div class="mc-options"><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="A"><strong>A</strong><span>W and X</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="B"><strong>B</strong><span>W and Z</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="C"><strong>C</strong><span>X and Y</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="D"><strong>D</strong><span>Y and Z</span></button></div><button class="check-answer">Check answer</button><p class="mc-feedback"></p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p><strong>D.</strong> Alkane halogenation is free-radical substitution; alkene bromination is electrophilic addition.</p></details>

### Question 11 · 3.2 Choice Medium Q1
<p>The cracking of one C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub> molecule produces two hydrocarbon molecules only. Each contains the same number of carbon atoms and has non-cyclic structural isomers. What is n?</p>
<div class="mc-options"><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="A"><strong>A</strong><span>10</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="B"><strong>B</strong><span>8</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="C"><strong>C</strong><span>6</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="D"><strong>D</strong><span>4</span></button></div><button class="check-answer">Check answer</button><p class="mc-feedback"></p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p><strong>B.</strong> Each product must have four carbons (the first chain length with structural isomers), so the parent has eight.</p></details>
:::

### Question 17 · 3.2 Choice Medium Q9
<p>0.200 mol of a hydrocarbon undergoes complete combustion to give 35.2 g CO<sub>2</sub> and 14.4 g H<sub>2</sub>O. What is its molecular formula?</p>
<div class="mc-options"><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="A"><strong>A</strong><span>C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub></span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="B"><strong>B</strong><span>C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub></span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="C"><strong>C</strong><span>C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>4</sub></span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="D"><strong>D</strong><span>C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub></span></button></div><button class="check-answer">Check answer</button><p class="mc-feedback"></p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p><strong>D.</strong> n(CO<sub>2</sub>)=35.2/44.0=0.800 mol, giving 0.800/0.200=4 carbon atoms. n(H<sub>2</sub>O)=14.4/18.0=0.800 mol, giving 2×0.800/0.200=8 hydrogen atoms.</p></details>
:::

### Question 20 · 3.2 Choice Hard Q7
![Polymer repeat unit used in the question](../assets/questions/extracted/14/independent/choice-hard-q7-polymer.png){.question-figure fig-alt="Polymer chain with hydroxyl groups on alternating carbon atoms"}
<p>A possible polymer has repeat unit –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH(OH)–. By which method might this polymer be made?</p>
<div class="mc-options"><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="A"><strong>A</strong><span>polymerise ethene followed by hydration</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="B"><strong>B</strong><span>polymerise ethene followed by oxidation with cold acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub></span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="C"><strong>C</strong><span>polymerise 1,2-dichloroethene followed by hydrolysis</span></button><button class="mc-choice" data-choice="D"><strong>D</strong><span>polymerise 1,2-dichloroethene followed by oxidation with cold acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub></span></button></div><button class="check-answer">Check answer</button><p class="mc-feedback"></p><details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show explanation</summary><p><strong>C.</strong> Hydrolysis replaces Cl by OH on the polymer chain.</p></details>
:::

## Structured questions

::: {.question-card #hc-sq-01}
### Question 1 · 3.2 SQ Easy Q1(a-d)
<p><strong>(a)</strong> State two reasons why alkanes are unreactive.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(i)</strong> Methane reacts with chlorine to produce chloromethane, CH<sub>3</sub>Cl. The reaction is initiated by the formation of chlorine radicals. State what is meant by a radical.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(ii)</strong> State the condition required to form chlorine free radicals from Cl<sub>2</sub>.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> State the type of bond fission involved in the reaction in part (b).</p>
<p><strong>(d)(i)</strong> Chloromethane will be formed via several steps. Write the equations for the two propagation steps.</p>
<p><strong>(d)(ii)</strong> Write an equation to show how ethane can be formed in this reaction.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ol><li>C–C/C–H bonds are strong (high bond enthalpy) and almost non-polar.</li><li>A radical is a species with an unpaired electron. UV light is required.</li><li>Homolytic fission: each atom takes one electron from the covalent bond.</li><li>Cl· + CH<sub>4</sub> → HCl + CH<sub>3</sub>·; CH<sub>3</sub>· + Cl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>Cl + Cl·.</li><li>CH<sub>3</sub>· + CH<sub>3</sub>· → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>; this is a termination step.</li></ol></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hc-sq-03}
### Question 2 · 3.2 SQ Easy Q2(a-d)
<img src="../assets/questions/extracted/14/independent/sq-easy-q2-mechanism.png" class="question-figure" alt="Propene reacting with hydrogen bromide through a carbocation intermediate" style="filter: invert(1);">
<p>This question is about the reactions of propene. Complete the flowchart below to show the major organic product formed in each of the addition reactions.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> Use ‘curly’ arrows to complete the mechanism for the formation of the major product when propene, CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub>, reacts with hydrogen bromide, HBr.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Draw the displayed formula of the minor product formed from the reaction of propene and hydrogen bromide.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> Explain why there is a major and minor product formed from the reaction between propene and hydrogen bromide.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li>Flowchart products: propan-2-ol with steam/acid catalyst; 1,2-dibromopropane with Br<sub>2</sub>; propane with H<sub>2</sub>/Ni.</li><li>The π bond attacks Hδ<sup>+</sup>, the H–Br bond breaks to Br<sup>−</sup>, and Br<sup>−</sup> attacks the secondary carbocation. The major product is 2-bromopropane.</li><li>The minor product is 1-bromopropane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br.</li><li>Both carbocations can form, but the secondary carbocation is more stable, so its pathway is favoured.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hc-sq-04}
### Question 3 · 3.2 SQ Easy Q3(a-d)
<p><strong>(a)</strong> State the difference between complete and incomplete combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel, such as octane. Include the balanced symbol equation for each in your answer.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(i)</strong> Octane is found in petrol. Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless and poisonous gas which is emitted in the exhaust fumes of motor vehicles that use a petrol internal combustion engine. State why carbon monoxide can cause dizziness, fainting, loss of consciousness and death in humans.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(ii)</strong> State another pollutant that is also released in cars’ exhaust fumes. Explain the effect of this pollutant in the atmosphere.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(i)</strong> Octane can be cracked to form pentane and one other product. Give the balanced symbol equation for this reaction.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(ii)</strong> Describe how catalytic cracking is carried out.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> Describe and give the result of a chemical test that would distinguish between the two products.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ol><li>Complete combustion uses sufficient O<sub>2</sub>: 2C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> + 25O<sub>2</sub> → 16CO<sub>2</sub> + 18H<sub>2</sub>O. Incomplete combustion has limited O<sub>2</sub>, for example 2C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> + 17O<sub>2</sub> → 16CO + 18H<sub>2</sub>O.</li><li>CO binds strongly to haemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport in the blood.</li><li>NO<sub>x</sub> contributes to acid rain/photochemical smog; unburnt hydrocarbons contribute to photochemical smog.</li><li>C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> → C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> + C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>; vaporise and pass over hot alumina/silica.</li><li>Bromine water: propene decolourises it; pentane shows no change without UV light.</li></ol></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hc-sq-06}
### Question 4 · 3.2 SQ Medium Q1(a-d)
![Fig. 4.1 Cyclohexane to chlorocyclohexane to cyclohexene](../assets/questions/extracted/14/independent/sq-medium-q1-fig-4-1.png){.question-figure fig-alt="Reaction scheme converting cyclohexane to chlorocyclohexane and then cyclohexene"}
![Table 4.1 Free-radical substitution mechanism](../assets/questions/extracted/14/independent/sq-medium-q1-table-4-1.png){.question-figure fig-alt="Completion table for initiation, propagation and termination steps"}
<p>A reaction scheme involving cyclohexane is shown in Fig. 4.1. Reaction 1 involves a free radical substitution mechanism.</p>
<p><strong>(a)</strong> State the essential condition required for reaction 1 to occur.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> Complete Table 4.1 to give details of the mechanism in reaction 1. Include curly arrows to show the movement of electrons occurring in the termination step.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Deduce the type of reaction that occurs in reaction 2.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> Hex-3-ene is an isomer of cyclohexane. Hex-3-ene can be converted into propanoic acid. Deduce the reagents and conditions for reaction 3.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ol><li>UV light/sunlight.</li><li>Initiation: Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2Cl·. Propagation: Cl· + C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub> → HCl + C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>11</sub>·; C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>11</sub>· + Cl<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>11</sub>Cl + Cl·. Termination: two radicals combine.</li><li>Elimination (dehydrohalogenation).</li><li>Hot concentrated acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>; oxidative cleavage of the central C=C produces two propanoic-acid molecules.</li></ol></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hc-sq-07}
### Question 5 · 3.2 SQ Medium Q2(a-d)
![Electrophilic addition prompt for pent-2-ene and hydrogen bromide](../assets/questions/extracted/14/independent/sq-medium-q2-mechanism.png){.question-figure fig-alt="Pent-2-ene and hydrogen bromide setup for drawing the electrophilic addition mechanism"}
<p>This question is about alkenes with the molecular formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>.</p>
<p><strong>(a)</strong> Draw the skeletal formulae of three branched-chain alkenes with the molecular formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(i)</strong> An alcohol can react with concentrated phosphoric acid, H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>, to form pent-2-ene. Give the formula of the alcohol that will form only pent-2-ene during this reaction.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(ii)</strong> Give a name for this type of reaction.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Pent-2-ene reacts with hydrogen bromide, HBr, to form two bromoalkanes. Complete the diagram to show the mechanism for the formation of 2-bromopentane. Include curly arrows, and relevant lone pairs and dipoles.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> A sample of pent-1-ene, with a mass of 1.33 g, is warmed to 60 °C in a sealed container. The volume of the container is 500 cm<sup>3</sup>. Calculate the pressure inside the container. Include units and give your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures. (R = 8.31 J mol<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup>.)</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ul><li>Draw three valid branched-chain alkenes, for example 2-methylbut-1-ene, 3-methylbut-1-ene and 2-methylbut-2-ene.</li><li>Pentan-3-ol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.</li><li>The reaction is elimination/dehydration.</li><li>Show electrophilic addition: π electrons attack Hδ<sup>+</sup>, H–Br breaks to Br<sup>−</sup>, then Br<sup>−</sup> attacks the carbocation.</li><li>n = 1.33/70.0 = 0.0190 mol; T = 333 K; V = 5.00 × 10<sup>−4</sup> m<sup>3</sup>; p = nRT/V = 1.05 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa.</li></ul></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hc-sq-08}
### Question 6 · 3.2 SQ Medium Q3(a-d)
<p>Crude oil contains a mixture of hydrocarbons which are separated using fractional distillation. Further processes can then be carried out, including cracking.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(i)</strong> What is meant by the term ‘cracking’?</p>
<p><strong>(a)(ii)</strong> Explain why cracking is carried out.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(i)</strong> State two conditions required for the cracking of alkanes.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(ii)</strong> Construct a balanced equation for the formation of heptane, C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub>, and two other products, by cracking tetradecane, C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>30</sub>.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(i)</strong> Another alkane, C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>, is used in gasoline. Explain why carbon monoxide is dangerous if inhaled.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(ii)</strong> Describe the environmental effect of oxides of nitrogen and unburnt hydrocarbons.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> Catalytic converters are found in the exhaust system of cars. Use equations to show how a catalytic converter reduces the levels of carbon monoxide and oxides of nitrogen released into the atmosphere.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ol><li>Cracking is thermal decomposition of large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller hydrocarbons. It is carried out to meet demand for smaller fuels and alkenes.</li><li>High temperature and a catalyst (or strong heating in thermal cracking).</li><li>One valid equation is C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>30</sub> → C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub> + C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>.</li><li>CO forms a stable complex with haemoglobin, preventing blood from carrying enough oxygen.</li><li>NO<sub>x</sub> and hydrocarbons react in sunlight to form photochemical smog; NO<sub>x</sub> also forms acids in rain.</li><li>2CO + 2NO → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + N<sub>2</sub>; 2CO + O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub>.</li></ol></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hc-sq-10}
### Question 7 · 3.2 SQ Medium Q4(a-d)
![Reaction flowchart for propene](../assets/questions/extracted/14/independent/sq-medium-q4-flowchart.png){.question-figure fig-alt="Flowchart showing propene reacting with steam, acidified potassium manganate(VII) and bromine"}
<p>This question is about alkanes and alkenes. Propene and propane can be produced from the cracking of hexane, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>.</p>
<p><strong>(a)</strong> Explain why propane is relatively unreactive.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> Describe and give the result of a test that can be done to distinguish between the two hydrocarbons.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(i)</strong> The reagents needed for three reactions of propene are shown in Fig. 4.1. Complete Fig. 4.1 by drawing the structure of the organic product produced in each reaction.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(ii)</strong> Propene also reacts with hydrogen bromide, HBr. Give the mechanism for this reaction to form the major product. Include curly arrows, and relevant lone pairs and dipoles.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> Propene reacts by addition polymerisation to form poly(propene). Draw the structure of poly(propene), showing two repeat units.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ol><li>Propane has strong C–C/C–H σ bonds with low polarity, so much energy is needed to break bonds and it has no electron-rich π bond.</li><li>Add bromine water: propene decolourises it; propane remains orange/brown under these conditions.</li><li>Steam gives propan-2-ol; cold dilute acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> gives propane-1,2-diol; bromine water gives 1-bromopropan-2-ol and 1,2-dibromopropane.</li><li>Correct repeat units are –CH<sub>2</sub>–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)– within continuation bonds.</li></ol></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hc-sq-11}
### Question 8 · 3.2 SQ Hard Q1(a-d)
<p>This question is about free radical substitution. 1,2-dibromoethane reacts with bromine in UV light to produce a mixture of further substituted haloalkanes.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(i)</strong> Write an equation for the initiation step.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(ii)</strong> Explain why this is an example of homolytic fission.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> Write two equations showing the propagation of this chain reaction to produce 1,1,2-tribromoethane.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(i)</strong> Traces of 1,2,3,4-tetrabromobutane are found in the reaction mixture. Write an equation to show how this product is formed.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(ii)</strong> Write a balanced symbol equation to show the overall reaction between 1,1,2-tribromoethane with bromine in UV light to form hexabromoethane.</p>
<p><strong>(d)</strong> Using the information from this question and your own knowledge, suggest the limitations of free radical substitution.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ol><li>Br<sub>2</sub> → 2Br· under UV light.</li><li>One electron from Br–Br goes to each Br atom, making two radicals.</li><li>Br· removes H, then the carbon radical reacts with Br<sub>2</sub>; show correct radical chain equations.</li><li>Radical coupling gives higher-mass products; continued substitution gives heavily brominated products.</li><li>It gives a mixture of products, may substitute at more than one position and makes separation difficult.</li></ol></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hc-sq-12}
### Question 9 · 3.2 SQ Hard Q2(a-c)
<p>This question is about hydrocarbons.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(i)</strong> Write an equation for the reaction between sodium hydroxide and carbon dioxide.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(ii)</strong> 10 cm<sup>3</sup> of a gaseous hydrocarbon, C<sub>x</sub>H<sub>y</sub>, is reacted with 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of oxygen gas, an excess. The final volume of the gaseous mixture is 95 cm<sup>3</sup>. After treatment with concentrated, aqueous sodium hydroxide, the volume is 75 cm<sup>3</sup>. Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide produced and the volume of oxygen used.</p>
<p><strong>(a)(iii)</strong> Use your answers, together with the initial volume of hydrocarbon, to balance the combustion equation and deduce x, y and z.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(i)</strong> A branched-chain hydrocarbon, W, with the formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, reacts with hydrogen bromide, HBr, to give two products X and Y. X and Y are structural isomers of molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>Br. More X is produced than Y. Give the structural formulae and names of W, X and Y.</p>
<p><strong>(b)(ii)</strong> When W reacts with hydrogen bromide, more X than Y is produced. Explain why.</p>
<p><strong>(c)</strong> Pent-2-ene will react with HBr. Draw the mechanism for the reaction of pent-2-ene with hydrogen bromide. You do not need to include any partial charges.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ol><li>CO<sub>2</sub> volume is 20 cm<sup>3</sup>; calculate O<sub>2</sub> used from the initial/final gas volumes and balance using volume ratios.</li><li>W is 2-methylpropene. Addition gives 2-bromo-2-methylpropane as the major product through the more stable tertiary carbocation, plus 1-bromo-2-methylpropane.</li><li>Show electrophilic addition: π electrons to H of HBr, C–H bond formation/carbocation, then Br<sup>−</sup> attack.</li></ol></details>
:::

::: {.question-card #hc-sq-13}
### Question 10 · 3.2 SQ Hard Q3(a-b)
<img src="../assets/questions/extracted/14/independent/sq-hard-q3-fig-3-1.png" class="question-figure" alt="Displayed structures comparing a mono-unsaturated oil with a polyunsaturated oil" style="filter: invert(1);">
<p>A student investigates the amount of C=C bonds in a molecule of cooking oil by titrating samples with bromine water.</p>
<p><strong>(a)</strong> Suggest two improvements that the student could make to the procedure to obtain more consistent results.</p>
<p><strong>(b)</strong> Use the student’s titration results, the approximate M<sub>r</sub> of the cooking oil, its density, the volume of one drop and the concentration of bromine water to deduce the number of C=C double bonds in a molecule of the oil. Show your working.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(i)</strong> Fig. 3.1 shows the structure of a mono-unsaturated oil and a polyunsaturated oil. Suggest what is meant by the terms mono-unsaturated oil and polyunsaturated.</p>
<p><strong>(c)(ii)</strong> Suggest the reagent and conditions necessary to produce the mono-unsaturated oil from the polyunsaturated oil.</p>
<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show mark scheme / model answer</summary><ol><li>Use a fixed measured volume/mass of oil rather than drops; repeat titrations and calculate a mean; use a consistent endpoint and accurate volumetric apparatus.</li><li>Find mean moles of Br<sub>2</sub>, calculate moles of oil from mass/M<sub>r</sub>, then use the 1:1 alkene:Br<sub>2</sub> ratio to find the number of C=C bonds.</li></ol></details>
:::
